title: Peptides Adsorption, fold and assemble on surfaces
teaser: A surface dictates how a peptide behaves. Through molecular simulations on metals and carbon nanomaterials, we study which residues anchor and which structures survive. These rules allow us to rationally design peptides that stabilize nanoparticles, coat surfaces, or self-assemble.
summary: A solid surface is not a passive support: the same peptide can keep its fold on one material and lose it on another. We simulate peptides and proteins on metals such as gold and silver, on carbon surfaces such as graphite and graphene, and on other nanomaterials, to learn which residues anchor, which secondary structure survives adsorption and when neighbouring chains order into layers. Those rules let us choose sequences that stabilize a nanoparticle, coat a surface or self-assemble on it.

title: What makes a nanoparticle choose a membrane
teaser: Overcoming the hydration shell to bind anions in water is a major challenge. We computationally design cyclic peptides and macrocycles for this task, transforming them into functionalized nanomaterials capable of removing water pollutants or capturing specific ions for mining.
summary: Wrapping a polymer core in lipids changes which cells a nanoparticle binds. We model hybrid lipid-polymer nanoparticles together with their target membranes to find what sets that selectivity; our recent work shows that lipid composition determines it, beyond simply mimicking the target membrane. Current theses extend this to the predictive design of lipid coatings, uptake by macrophages and photocontrollable carriers for colorectal cancer.

title: Capturing anions with peptides and macrocycles
teaser: Peptides and macrocycles as receptors for anions such as phosphate, in solution or grafted to a surface.
summary: Binding an anion selectively in water is difficult, because the receptor has to compete with the ion's hydration shell. We design receptors for that job, cyclic peptides and other macrocycles, and compute how strongly and how selectively each one binds its target against the other ions in solution. Grafted onto a nanosurface, these receptors become materials that remove anionic pollutants such as phosphate and nitrate from water, or that capture and release ions in mining processes.
alt: Close-up render of peptide chains lying on a flat surface with small ions above them.

title: Ion channels, lipids and peptide materials
teaser: Simulations alongside experiments on channel regulation, membrane-active peptides and peptide hydrogels.
summary: Much of our work runs alongside experimental groups. Together we have described a peripheral PIP2-binding site that regulates TRP channels, the temperature dependence of charybdotoxin binding to Shaker K+ channels, and the electrostatic bridges that drive crosslinking of collagen-like peptides, and we have contributed simulations to peptide hydrogels for tissue repair. A current thesis studies how hydrophobic and cationic residues cooperate in antimicrobial peptides at lipid membranes.
